tagline: Twenty-two signs trace Solomon Northup’s Louisiana journey from Alexandria to Marksville.
intro: The Northup Trail links Alexandria and Marksville across 83 miles, with 22 signs marking its stops. This Louisiana Scenic Byway includes US 71 between Alexandria and Bunkie, passing through Lecompte on Bayou Boeuf. The Louisiana Office of Tourism presents it as a journey through Solomon Northup’s story and suggests two days for the trail. The country surrounding Bunkie is agricultural, while the trail’s stops include plantation sites, Bayou Boeuf and the offices connected with Northup’s release.

Northup was a free-born African American farmer and professional violinist from New York. An offer of traveling musical work took him to Washington in 1841, where he was kidnapped and sold into slavery. He remained enslaved in central Louisiana until 1853, then returned to New York and wrote Twelve Years a Slave. Later, researchers Sue Eakin and Joseph Logsdon checked the people and events in his memoir and published an annotated edition in 1968.

Start at Alexandria’s Red River Landing, where Northup disembarked from the steamer Rodolf after being sold in New Orleans. Continue to the reconstructed Epps House at Louisiana State University at Alexandria, then through the trail’s Cheneyville, Bunkie and Evergreen stops. The journey ends in Marksville, where papers recognizing Northup’s freedom were signed at the Avoyelles Parish courthouse in 1853.

moments.title: Epps House
moments.text: Solomon Northup helped build Edwin Epps’s Creole cottage on Bayou Boeuf in 1852 while Epps held him enslaved. During that year, Northup confided in Canadian carpenter Samuel Bass, who sent letters seeking help from New York. The house has since moved twice: to Bunkie in 1976, then to LSU Alexandria in 1999. At the second move it was dismantled and reconstructed, with some original materials replaced. A room is dedicated to Northup’s story. Historian Sue Eakin located the house while investigating the accuracy of Northup’s memoir, connecting his written testimony to the building he helped construct.

moments.title: Cheneyville
moments.text: William Prince Ford links Cheneyville’s religious history to Northup’s enslavement. Ford bought Northup in New Orleans in 1841, after Northup had been kidnapped in Washington. Two years later, influenced by Alexander Campbell’s writings, Ford led most of a Baptist congregation into the Church of Christ. The Cheneyville Christian Church is Louisiana’s oldest congregation associated with the Restoration Movement. The trail also includes Historic Cheneyville and Trinity Episcopal Church among its stops.

moments.title: Marksville
moments.text: In early 1853, Henry Northup arrived in Marksville and sought help from local attorney John P. Waddill. Together with the sheriff, the attorneys went to the Epps plantation on Bayou Boeuf to find Solomon Northup. Papers recognizing his freedom were signed at the Avoyelles Parish courthouse that January. The courthouse now in the commercial historic district dates to 1927: a four-story brick building in Classical Revival style. It is a later building than the courthouse of Northup’s release. Northup returned to New York and published his memoir that same year, preserving his account of the kidnapping and years of enslavement.
